title: Is rejection good for us?
intro: How would you feel about going up to a stranger on the street and asking them for a cheeky favour? If the idea makes you nervous, then don't worry – you are not alone! But recently, some people have been filming themselves doing this, as part of a social media trend called 'rejection therapy'. It's not an officially recognised form of therapy, but some have found that it improves their confidence. Georgie and Neil discuss this and teach you some new vocabulary.
this_week_question: Which of these things did not happen to the animator Walt Disney before he became successful?
a) he lost his job as an artist b) his first business ran out of money c) his first full length film was a failure
Listen to the programme to hear the answer.

transcript.text: Well, nobody likes rejection . But I think as you get older, you get used to it. And probably it's quite a good thing to experience rejection , even if it doesn't feel nice.

transcript.text: OK. That sounds quite interesting, but let's find out how it works in practice. Hannah Gelbart, host of the BBC World Service podcast What in the World, had a go at the trend. Let's see how she got on.

transcript.text: Yeah.

transcript.text: Good, thank you.

transcript.text: Well, it seems like people were pretty nice to Hannah in those examples.

transcript.author: Neil

transcript.text: Hannah says that when she walked up to the first stranger in the video, she felt her adrenaline spiking . If something spikes , it increases sharply.

transcript.author: Neil
transcript.text: Hannah is not generally a socially anxious person. Someone who is socially anxious is nervous or worried about speaking to other people.

transcript.author: Georgie
transcript.text: Each time Hannah tried to speak to a new person, she says, it came easier . Come easier is an informal way to say something is easier to achieve.

transcript.author: Georgie
transcript.text: Psychologist Claudia Hammond has some ideas, which she shared with Hannah on the BBC World Service podcast What in the World.

transcript.text: What we do know is that there is an increase in perfectionism . People are more worried now, younger people, about how other people are judging them. transcript.text: Claudia says there's an increase in perfectionism among young people. Perfectionism is the feeling that everything you do needs to be perfect.

transcript.author: Georgie

transcript.author: Neil
transcript.text: Deliberately looking for rejection might be an extreme way to become more confident, but it can lead to surprising discoveries.
